question: According to the EU’s European Solar PV Industry Alliance, the EU is aiming to achieve 30 GW of manufacturing capacity for all links in the solar energy supply chain by 2025, resulting in 400 000 new, green jobs and greater independence from China, which is the dominant market player. Regrettably, at present it looks virtually impossible to realise that objective.

The reason for European solar producers’ plight is that, for a long time, China has been engaging in market dumping driven by subsidies, poor environmental practices and the documented use of forced labour in the Xinjiang region. Fifteen years ago, Europe accounted for some 40% of solar panel production; today the figure is less than 5%.

China now accounts for more than 80% – even more in other sections of the supply chain. Solar energy is forecast to be the world’s greatest source of power in a few decades’ time. At the same time, however, making ourselves so dependent on the world’s largest dictatorship is totally unsustainable. 1.

Since the Commission is not ruling out taking trade protection measures, does it intend to do any analysis of its own, with the possibility of action, on the Chinese dumping of the market for solar cell materials?
When can we expect to see the new, green jobs in the EU as a result of aggressive efforts to bring PV manufacturing back to Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.6.2024) The Commission is committed to a robust use of trade defence instruments (TDI) to protect EU industry from unfair and injurious trading practices where warranted. EU rules on TDI require to assess the injury suffered by EU producers from unfair imports and the EU’s overall interest to impose such a measure.

The fact that, today, the bulk of the demand for solar modules in Europe is covered by imports from China would be an important factor in the assessment of the Union interest and the potential impact of any TDI measure on photovoltaic (PV) modules deployment. Should the Commission receive a duly substantiated request, it will analyse it and take action as appropriate.

In December 2022, the Commission launched the European Solar Industry Alliance1 to reach the target of 30 gigawatts of European manufacturing capacity by 20302: through an announced solid project pipeline, the Alliance would enable to create 400 000 jobs.

In March 2023, the large-scale renewable energy skills partnership was launched in order to empower workers with the skills needed for manufacturing and managing renewable energy technologies, including solar PV, to meet EU targets3. The Net-Zero Industry Act4 includes provisions to enhance skills, through Net-Zero Industry Academies in strategic net-zero technology sectors.

On solar PV technologies, the launch of a skills Academy5 aims to support the up- and reskilling of the required EU sector workforce6. The Academy is mandated to train 100 000 workers within three years from its establishment. Lastly, in April 2024, the Commission, 23 Member States and industry representatives signed the European Solar Charter7.
It sets out voluntary actions to further support the competitiveness of the EU PV manufacturing sector.
